article_title: Do Low-Income Students have Equal Access to the Highest-Performing Teachers?
citation: Steven Glazerman and Jeffrey Max. (2011). Do Low-Income Students Have Equal Access to the Highest-Performing Teachers? NCEE Evaluation Brief, NCEE 2011-4016. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/pubs/20114016/pdf/20114016_app.pdf
title: Policymakers concerned with equitable access to teacher quality should attend to the distribution of teacher effectiveness measured by classroom performance, not credentials
description: The brief argues that because credentials inequitably distributed across schools are only weakly associated with classroom performance, equity policy should target performance-based measures. It states that those who want to assure disadvantaged students have access to teachers at least as good "need to attend to the distribution of teacher effectiveness, measured in terms of classroom performance, rather than to the distribution of teacher credentials." As policy shifts toward performance measures, information on the distribution of high-performing teachers can help assure the best teachers are deployed where most needed.
requirements: District data systems that measure teacher effectiveness through value-added analysis of student achievement growth
constraints: Findings pertain to ten purposefully selected large districts and are not necessarily applicable to other districts
Few districts systematically collect or use data on teacher effectiveness
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to high-performing teachers
examples: The brief analyzed prevalence of top-20-percent value-added teachers across school poverty quintiles in ten districts to inform such equity policy
key_sources: Steven Glazerman and Jeffrey Max. (2011). Do Low-Income Students Have Equal Access to the Highest-Performing Teachers? NCEE Evaluation Brief, NCEE 2011-4016. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/pubs/20114016/pdf/20114016_app.pdf

article_title: Temporal Network Analysis of Collaborative Prototyping from a Knowledge Creation Perspective
citation: Ohsaki, A., Tan, Y., Eagan, B., Shaffer, D. W., & Swiecki, Z. (2026). Temporal Network Analysis of Collaborative Prototyping from a Knowledge Creation Perspective. Journal of Learning Analytics, 13(1), 190–207. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2026.8959
title: Attend to disciplinary differences when facilitating interdisciplinary knowledge creation teams
description: This principle holds that educators facilitating knowledge creation in interdisciplinary teams should recognize that different disciplines bring distinct epistemic agency patterns to collaborative work. The article states educators may "grasp the characteristics of different disciplines, determine the timing of interventions, and design scaffolding" accordingly. It emerged from finding that engineers, product designers, and service designers showed significantly different KC patterns during prototyping.
requirements: Educators need awareness of disciplinary frameworks shaping team members' collaborative problem-solving approaches
constraints: Based on analysis of three teams from three specific disciplines in a Japanese educational context
target_learning_goals: knowledge creation
collaborative problem-solving
examples: The study compared engineering, product design, and service design teams during wallet prototyping, finding distinct epistemic agency patterns for each discipline
key_sources: Ohsaki, A., Tan, Y., Eagan, B., Shaffer, D. W., & Swiecki, Z. (2026). Temporal Network Analysis of Collaborative Prototyping from a Knowledge Creation Perspective. Journal of Learning Analytics, 13(1), 190–207. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2026.8959

article_title: 7 Recommendations for Using Education Data to Support Equitable Learning Outcomes
citation: Jessica Arnold, Julie Webb. (2024). 7 Recommendations for Using Education Data to Support Equitable Learning Outcomes. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Attend to data quality before placing stock in an analysis, because high-quality data are a prerequisite for meaningful analysis
description: This principle instructs users not to take data at face value but to first examine how data were collected, managed, and retrieved. The brief asserts that "High-quality data are a prerequisite for any meaningful data analysis effort." It gives concrete checks: understanding the design, purpose, and administration of an assessment before analyzing results, and considering survey design and respondent representativeness before interpreting survey results.
requirements: Before analysis, establish how the data were collected, managed, and retrieved; for assessments, understand design, purpose, and administration; for surveys, consider design and respondent representativeness
target_learners: all students whose outcomes are measured by assessments and surveys
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of assessment and survey results
examples: The brief's example checks cover assessment data and survey data specifically
key_sources: Jessica Arnold, Julie Webb. (2024). 7 Recommendations for Using Education Data to Support Equitable Learning Outcomes. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655653

article_title: When AI Tutors Speak: Evidence from a Randomized Field Experiment
citation: Shihao Yang, Marshall Van Alstyne, and Chrysanthos Dellarocas. (2026). When AI Tutors Speak: Evidence from a Randomized Field Experiment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23958
title: Attempt-first structured tutoring cycle with Bloom laddering and a transfer capstone
description: The article's treatment is a pedagogical cycle enforced by the tutor's system prompt, not the underlying model. The tutor opens with retrieval warm-up on prior material, draws questions from the week's learning objectives ordered up Bloom's ladder, and "posesone question at a timeand requiresanattemptbeforeitwillexplain;thisistheprompt'scentralrule." On error it scaffolds with a smaller step, graduated hint, or a worked example followed by an isomorphic variant; errors receive targeted feedback written to a persistent blackboard the student can export. A topic is complete only when the student answers an unassisted transfer question, then the session advances one Bloom rung up. The authors map attempt-first questioning to retrieval practice, the Bloom ladder with transfer capstone to the SOLO relational threshold, and required production on every turn to the production and self-explanation channels, operationalizing the interactive tier of the ICAP hierarchy.
requirements: A course-specific knowledge base (weekly readings, lecture notes, problem sets) to ground the tutor
A rule-dense pedagogical prompt the LLM follows reliably on every turn
Structured tool-calling so the tutor can write to the shared blackboard
constraints: The cycle operates identically in both channels, so it isolates pedagogy from delivery modality by design
It was deployed as an optional, ungraded weekly practice layer barred from graded-assessment content
target_learners: Working-professional online MBA students in a quantitative corporate-finance module
target_learning_goals: Quantitative finance problem-solving (NPV, discount rates, cost of capital) with conceptual depth at SOLO relational level or better
examples: The deployed tutor diagnosed before explaining, required an attempt, scaffolded errors with smaller steps rather than answers, consolidated worked results to the blackboard, and closed topics only on unassisted transfer (Figure 3)
key_sources: Shihao Yang, Marshall Van Alstyne, and Chrysanthos Dellarocas. (2026). When AI Tutors Speak: Evidence from a Randomized Field Experiment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23958

article_title: Profiling cognitive offloading in LLM-mediated synthesis writing: Volume vs. content
citation: Poquet, O., Nanduri, M. S., Salinas Loyer, M. X., Stadler, M., Sailer, M., Jovanovic, J. (2026). Profiling Cognitive Offloading in LLM-mediated Synthesis Writing: Volume vs. Content. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10434
title: Interventions should attend to what learners delegate to LLMs, not just limit the volume of LLM use
description: Because the same volume of LLM use can describe qualitatively different offloading processes, the article argues that "interventions targeting the volume of LLM use, such as limiting the number of prompts, may be insuffi- cient". More targeted approaches attend to whether learners retain active involvement in structuring and evaluating, or hand off entire segments of the comprehension process. Tools making the distribution of cognitive work visible to learners and instructors could support this, though evaluation is still needed.
requirements: Means of characterising prompt content (who performs the activity, at what comprehension level) so that delegation patterns can be distinguished
constraints: The article states more work is needed to evaluate offloading processes and their differentiated effects, and whether fragmentation patterns predict learning outcomes directly and hold across tasks with different cognitive demands
target_learners: university students using general-purpose LLM chatbots for academic writing
target_learning_goals: retaining active comprehension and knowledge construction during LLM-mediated writing
examples: The study showed Strategic and Full Offloading involved similarly high prompting volumes but very different learner engagement, which volume-based profiling did not convey
key_sources: Poquet, O., Nanduri, M. S., Salinas Loyer, M. X., Stadler, M., Sailer, M., Jovanovic, J. (2026). Profiling Cognitive Offloading in LLM-mediated Synthesis Writing: Volume vs. Content. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10434

article_title: EduGage: Methods and Dataset for Sensor-Based Momentary Assessment of Engagement in Self-Guided Video Learning
citation: Zikang Leng, Edan Eyal, Yingtian Shi, Jiaman He, Yaqi Liu, and Thomas Plötz. (2026). EduGage: A Multimodal Dataset and Benchmark for Sensor-Based Momentary Assessment of Engagement in Self-Guided Video Learning. Proc. ACM Interact. Mob. Wearable Ubiquitous Ubiquitous Technol. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01238
title: Engagement-probe ratings as a pragmatic single-item operationalization of the attentional aspect of momentary engagement
description: The article frames its single-item probe ("How difficult was it to pay attention during the last minute of the lecture?") as a temporally localized reference signal targeting perceived difficulty sustaining attention, explicitly not equivalent to engagement as a whole. The authors write that they use it "as a narrower, engagement-related attentional experience rather than as engagement itself or its direct inverse", recognizing that a learner may remain engaged with demanding material while finding attention hard to sustain.
requirements: Repeated in-situ administration at approximately one-minute intervals placed at natural stopping points in the content, with a short practice phase so participants learn the scale before the main task
constraints: The single-item measure is not intended to reproduce comprehensive multidimensional engagement instruments; its narrower construct coverage is acknowledged as a limitation
target_learners: college students in self-guided video learning
target_learning_goals: momentary perceived difficulty of sustaining attention during instruction
examples: During the study, the video paused at each probe and the screen displayed the abbreviated cue "Report engagement now," with participants responding on the 1–5 scale learned during training

article_title: Interaction Effects Between Learner Characteristics and Dialogue Format in TTS Dialogue-Based Lessons
citation: Fumie Watanabe, Tota Suko, Takashi Ishida, Yuko Kuma, Manabu Kobayashi, Shigeichi Hirasawa, and Gendo Kumoi. (2026). Interaction Effects Between Learner Characteristics and Dialogue Format in TTS Dialogue-Based Lessons. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20822
title: Aptitude-Treatment Interaction as the framework for matching dialogue format to learner characteristics
description: The article applies the Aptitude-Treatment Interaction (ATI) framework, in which "learning outcomes are jointly determined by the combination of learner characteristics (aptitude) and instructional method (treatment)". Learner characteristics — the CE and RCE factors of experiential learning style and critical thinking disposition — serve as aptitudes, while the three LLM+TTS dialogue formats (TS, SS, TT) serve as treatments. The framework motivates examining which format is more effective for learners with which style, and grounds the study's recommendation to personalize format selection.
requirements: Measurement of learner characteristics (experiential learning style, critical thinking disposition) alongside multiple instructional formats under comparable conditions
constraints: The article notes detecting interaction effects generally requires a larger sample size than detecting main effects
target_learning_goals: data science literacy and data-driven career education content
examples: The study treated dialogue format as the ATI treatment and experiential learning style as the aptitude across three TTS dialogue lesson formats viewed by 222 students

article_title: Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators.
citation: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000209
title: Attentional bias framework (sequential attention theory) of interleaved learning
description: The attentional bias framework, also called sequential attention theory, explains positional-relations effects in inductive learning by what presentation format highlights: "an interleaved presentation highlights differences between items, whereas a blocked presentation highlights similarities." Interleaving is therefore predicted to be better when between-category differences are crucial (low-discriminability, highly similar exemplars), and blocking better when within-category similarities are crucial (high-discriminability exemplars). The meta-analysis used this framework to motivate its similarity and complexity moderators.
requirements: Applies to inductive category learning where success depends on discriminating exemplars from different categories
constraints: The framework predicts a blocking advantage in high-discriminability conditions where within-category similarities are crucial
target_learning_goals: inductive category learning and category discrimination
examples: The meta-analysis coded rater-based within- and between-category similarity ratings of 71 material sets and tested them as moderators of the interleaving effect.
key_sources: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000209

article_title: A systematic review of interleaving as a concept learning strategy
citation: Jonathan Firth, Ian Rivers and James Boyle. (2021). A systematic review of interleaving as a concept learning strategy. Review of Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/rev3.3266
title: Attentional accounts of the interleaving effect: attention attenuation and attentional bias
description: The review describes two related attentional explanations. The attention-attenuation hypothesis (Wahlheim, Dunlosky, and Jacoby, 2011) holds that "blocking is inferior because attention dwindles when learners see repeated examples of the same type", supported by Metcalfe and Xu's (2016) mind-wandering probes showing more mind wandering in blocked conditions. The attentional-bias hypothesis (Carvalho and Goldstone) holds that interleaving directs attention to between-category differences while blocking directs attention to within-category similarities, implying the similarity of examples may matter as much as order.
requirements: Learners must attend to contrasts between adjacent examples for the interleaving benefit to arise
constraints: Attentional-bias account implies classroom application is highly context specific, drawing on teachers' professional knowledge of the material
target_learning_goals: inductive concept learning
sustained attention during example study
examples: Metcalfe and Xu (2016) presented paintings with a mind-wandering probe and found mind wandering at a higher level during the blocked condition
key_sources: Jonathan Firth, Ian Rivers and James Boyle. (2021). A systematic review of interleaving as a concept learning strategy. Review of Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/rev3.3266

article_title: When you know that you know and when you think that you know but you don’t
citation: Zechmeister, E. B., & Shaughnessy, J. J. (1980). When you know that you know and when you think that you know but you don't. Bulletin of the Psychonomic Society, 15(1), 41-44. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03334497
title: Attenuation of attention hypothesis with an overconfidence basis: learners underprocess massed repetitions because they believe massed items are already known
description: The attenuation of attention hypothesis explains the spacing effect by asserting that "learners pay less atten­tion to massed repetitions than to distributed repetit ions" because massed repetitions occur near the item's initial presentation. This article supplies the missing reason for that inattention: retrieved ease at a massed repetition gives undue confidence of memory strength, so learners judge MP items as already learned and skip further processing. The MP-over-DP rating overconfidence found in the experiment supports this account.
requirements: The learner must make (implicit or explicit) judgments about an item's encoding status at the time of a massed repetition
constraints: The article notes results are equally consistent with underestimation of recall likelihood for DP items rather than overestimation for MP items
Further study is needed, per the authors, to determine factors that facilitate or retard accuracy of judging what is known
target_learning_goals: free recall of verbal items
calibration of self-assessment of learning during study
examples: Subjects rated MP items as more recallable than DP items in every study block while recalling them less well, supporting the assumption that the inattention to massed presentations stems from overestimating memory for them
key_sources: Zechmeister, E. B., & Shaughnessy, J. J. (1980). When you know that you know and when you think that you know but you don't. Bulletin of the Psychonomic Society, 15(1), 41-44. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03329756

article_title: Working Memory and Attention – A Conceptual Analysis and Review
citation: Oberauer, K. (2019). Working Memory and Attention – A Conceptual Analysis and Review. Journal of Cognition, 2(1): 36. https://doi.org/10.5334/joc.58
title: A three-dimensional taxonomy organizing concepts of attention by definition, objects, and mode of control
description: The review proposes a coordinate system for organizing concepts of attention along three dimensions. The first distinguishes attention as a limited resource from attention as "a process of (or mechanism for) selection of information to be processed with priority". The second distinguishes objects of attention along two sub-dimensions (perceptual vs. non-perceptual; things/events vs. goals/actions). The third distinguishes controlled from automatic deployment. Table 1 displays the resulting cells, each describing a distinct form of attention.
requirements: The taxonomy requires distinguishing how attention is defined from what attention is directed at and from what determines its orientation
constraints: The review notes the term executive attention is ambiguously used across two of these dimensions and proposes replacing it with attention to cognitive action and controlled attention
target_learning_goals: understanding the conceptual structure of attention theories
understanding how attention concepts relate to working memory theory
examples: Table 1 in the article displays cells such as selective attention to locations, visual objects, events, features and capture of attention by salient stimuli
key_sources: Oberauer, K. (2019). Working Memory and Attention – A Conceptual Analysis and Review. Journal of Cognition, 2(1): 36. https://doi.org/10.5334/joc.58

article_title: Neurocognitive mechanisms underlying working memory encoding and retrieval in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
citation: Ortega, R., López, V., Carrasco, X., Escobar, M. J., García, A. M., Parra, M. A. & Aboitiz, F. (2020). Neurocognitive mechanisms underlying working memory encoding and retrieval in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder. Scientific Reports 10:7771. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-64678-x
title: Attention-guided prioritization and updating account of WM impairment in ADHD: binding intact, encoding and retrieval compromised
description: The article proposes that WM impairment in ADHD arises not from deficient binding or early visual filtering but from compromised attention-dependent encoding and retrieval. It draws on the context updating theory of P3, in which "P3 amplitude reflects the effort to continuously update new relevant information to the representation held in WM", and on resource-allocation accounts. Reduced encoding P3, retrieval P3 that fails to discriminate change, and absent encoding-retrieval P3 correlations in ADHD are read as "a failure in the prioritization of relevant information". The account informs theories of binding in visual WM by showing bound features are held intact despite attentional impairment.
requirements: ERP measurement separating encoding and retrieval stages, as behavioral responses alone cannot discriminate WM stages
constraints: Inferences limited by sample size, possible implicit verbal rehearsal, ADHD heterogeneity, and medication effects, per the authors' limitations section
target_learning_goals: understanding working memory encoding, binding and retrieval processes in attentional disorders
examples: A visual short-term memory binding task with no nameable polygons and non-primary colors, spatial locations interchanged between study and test displays, used with 18 ADHD and 18 matched non-ADHD adolescents
key_sources: Ortega, R., López, V., Carrasco, X., Escobar, M. J., García, A. M., Parra, M. A. & Aboitiz, F. (2020). Neurocognitive mechanisms underlying working memory encoding and retrieval in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder. Scientific Reports 10:7771. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-64678-x

article_title: How bilingualism modulates selective attention in children
citation: Jacqueline Phelps, Adam Attaheri & Mirjana Bozic. (2022). How bilingualism modulates selective attention in children. Scientific Reports 12:6381. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-09989-x
title: Resource-economisation account of bilingual neurocognitive adaptation
description: The article proposes that language selection and inhibition in bilinguals themselves draw on a finite selective attention capacity, so remaining resources must be economised to support optimal task performance. It predicts "no increase—or possibly even a slight reduction" in neural indices of attentional processing combined with a different distribution across task conditions, rather than the enhancement predicted by the bilingual-advantage view. The study's findings of equivalent behaviour with a flatter, overall weaker encoding pattern in bilinguals are read as supporting this redistribution account, extending the adaptive control hypothesis.
requirements: Bilingual language use must impose constant management of competing languages, creating processing demands that draw on attentional resources
constraints: The interpretation of reduced encoding in weak-interference conditions as economisation is described by the authors as tentative
target_learning_goals: selective attention as a foundational skill for academic success
examples: Children attended to English narratives while ignoring English, Latin, or Musical Rain interference; bilinguals showed weaker encoding only where interference was weakest
key_sources: Jacqueline Phelps, Adam Attaheri & Mirjana Bozic. (2022). How bilingualism modulates selective attention in children. Scientific Reports 12:6381. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-09989-x

article_title: Metacognition and motivation as predictors for mathematics performance of Belgian elementary school children
citation: Desoete, A., Baten, E., Vercaemst, V., De Busschere, A., Baudonck, M., & Vanhaeke, J. (2019). Metacognition and motivation as predictors for mathematics performance of Belgian elementary school children. ZDM Mathematics Education, 51, 667–677. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-018-01020-w
title: Teachers should attend to both mathematical accuracy and fluency, and to metacognitive and motivational aspects, especially for poor performers
description: The article's practical recommendation, drawn from its longitudinal finding that accuracy and fluency have "overlapping yet different predictors", is that teachers pay attention to both aspects of mathematics. Because poor performers were found to be less intrinsically motivated, less metacognitively accurate, and to overestimate their performances more often than well-performing peers in all grades, the authors stress the importance of attending to these metacognitive and motivational aspects in mathematics education.
requirements: Instruction should address both accuracy and fluency as partly distinct outcome aspects of mathematics learning.
constraints: The recommendation rests on the study's Belgian elementary sample tested in January and June; the motivation–accuracy relation was reported for Grade 3.
target_learning_goals: Mathematical accuracy
Mathematical fluency
Metacognitive accuracy of performance evaluation
Intrinsic motivation for mathematics
examples: The study tested Belgian children from Grade 1 till 6 in January and June and derived the recommendation from the differing predictor sets for accuracy and fluency.
key_sources: Desoete, A., Baten, E., Vercaemst, V., De Busschere, A., Baudonck, M., & Vanhaeke, J. (2019). Metacognition and motivation as predictors for mathematics performance of Belgian elementary school children. ZDM Mathematics Education, 51, 667–677. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-018-01020-w

article_title: Effects of acute bouts of physical activity on children's attention: a systematic review of the literature
citation: Janssen M, Toussaint HM, van Mechelen W, Verhagen EALM. (2014). Effects of acute bouts of physical activity on children's attention: a systematic review of the literature. SpringerPlus. https://doi.org/10.1186/2193-1801-3-410
title: Attention as a gate into working memory mediating PA effects on cognition
description: The review organizes its inquiry around attention defined as "the ability to resist distraction", acting as a gate regulating the flow of sensory information into working memory and conscious awareness. It frames attention as required both for encoding new information and for recalling memories, and as a mediator between physical activity and academic achievement, since deficits in attention are associated with poorer academic performance. This framing justifies focusing the review solely on attention as the outcome measure.
requirements: Attention must be measurable; the review notes attention is always involved in other cognitive processes, making its measurement difficult
constraints: The definition of attention is not unambiguous; selective, divided and sustained attention are distinguished theoretically
target_learning_goals: attention and cognitive control supporting learning and memory
examples: The review used this framework to justify excluding studies of other cognitive outcomes such as memory or successive processing

article_title: Attentional Control Buffers the Effect of Public-Speaking Anxiety on Performance
citation: Jones Christopher R., Fazio Russell H., Vasey Michael W. (2012). Attentional Control Buffers the Effect of Public Speaking Anxiety on Performance. Social Psychological and Personality Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/1948550611430166
title: Attentional control theory: anxiety impairs performance by hampering goal-directed attentional processes
description: Attentional control theory, cited from Eysenck, Derakshan, Santos, and Calvo (2007), distinguishes between two relevant attentional systems. As the article states, it "posits that anxiety impairs cognitive performance by hampering goal-directed attentional processes while leaving stimulus-driven processes that respond to environmental cues relatively intact." This disruption leads to increased attention capture by salient stimuli, especially threatening ones. The article uses this framework to motivate the prediction that individuals with greater attentional control capacity should be better equipped to deal with anxiety produced by public speaking.
requirements: The framework presupposes that effective performance on demanding tasks depends on goal-directed attentional processes that must be maintained against stimulus-driven capture.
target_learners: adult learners performing anxiety-inducing public speaking or other demanding cognitive tasks
target_learning_goals: maintaining task performance under anxiety by regulating attention toward goal-directed processes
examples: The study measured attentional control with the 20-item Attentional Control Scale and tested the theory's moderating prediction in a public speaking task.
key_sources: Jones Christopher R., Fazio Russell H., Vasey Michael W. (2012). Attentional Control Buffers the Effect of Public Speaking Anxiety on Performance. Social Psychological and Personality Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/1948550611430166

article_title: Cognitive Flexibility and Theory of Mind Outcomes Among Foster Children: Preschool Follow-Up Results of a Randomized Clinical Trial
citation: Lewis-Morrarty, E., Dozier, M., Bernard, K., Terracciano, S., & Moore, S. (2012). Cognitive Flexibility and Theory of Mind Outcomes Among Foster Children: Preschool Follow-up Results of a Randomized Clinical Trial. Journal of Adolescent Health. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jadohealth.2012.05.005
title: Attachment and Biobehavioral Catch-up (ABC) intervention
description: The ABC intervention is a "10-session, manualized parenting program aimed at enhancing young children’s self-regulatory capacities by helping caregivers provide nurturing and synchronous care." Interventionists explain the developmental research basis, videotape parent-child interactions so caregivers can practice "following the child’s lead," give video feedback highlighting nurturing versus intrusive or disengaged moments, and help caregivers reflect on how their own early experiences may hinder nurturing care. In this study it was delivered to foster parents of infants and toddlers and evaluated against a control intervention.
requirements: Trained interventionists who deliver the 10 manualized sessions, including video feedback of parent-child interactions
constraints: In this trial it was delivered to parents of foster children placed before age three, prior to 20 months of age
target_learners: Foster parents and other caregivers of infants and toddlers who have experienced early adversity
target_learning_goals: Providing nurturing care in response to child distress
Engaging in synchronous parent-child interactions that support children's self-regulatory development
examples: Foster children randomly assigned to ABC before age 20 months were assessed at ages 4–6 on the Dimensional Change Card Sort and the penny-hiding game

article_title: The effects of preexposure to a nonattended stimulus on subsequent learning: Latent inhibition in adults
citation: A. Ginton, G. Urca, and R. E. Lubow. (1975). The effects of preexposure to a nonattended stimulus on subsequent learning: Latent inhibition in adults. Bulletin of the Psychonomic Society, 1975, Vol. 5 (1), 5-8.
title: Attentional account of latent inhibition: lack of an attentional response to the CS at the start of the learning phase is the necessary condition for latent inhibition
description: The article proposes that the necessary condition for producing latent inhibition is the lack of an attentional response to the to-be-conditioned stimulus in the formal learning phase. Nonreinforced preexposure is described as sufficient for infrahumans and children but insufficient for adults, because adult subjects' expectation that something will happen with the tone may increase over presentations. The account holds that masking reduces the stimulus' salience and thereby enhances the occurrence of inattention, and that acquired inattention develops through the preexposure phase as the attentional response diminishes with repeated presentations.
requirements: The preexposure phase must be constructed so the to-be-conditioned stimulus is exposed within a masking situation which provides a plausible explanation for the presence of the stimulus
constraints: Nonreinforced preexposure alone is described as insufficient for producing latent inhibition in adults without a masking situation
target_learning_goals: conditioned responding to a previously nonreinforced stimulus
examples: The experiment embedded the white-noise CS within a dichotic listening task so it could be perceived as part of the background noise
key_sources: A. Ginton, G. Urca, and R. E. Lubow. (1975). The effects of preexposure to a nonattended stimulus on subsequent learning: Latent inhibition in adults. Bulletin of the Psychonomic Society, 1975, Vol. 5 (1), 5-8. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03336682

article_title: Developmental Dyscalculia in Adults
citation: Liane Kaufmann, Michael von Aster, Silke M. Göbel, Josef Marksteiner, and Elise Klein. (2020). Developmental Dyscalculia in Adults: Current Issues and Open Questions for Future Research. Lernen und Lernstörungen, 9(2), 126–137. https://doi.org/10.1024/2235-0977/a000294
title: ATOM: A Theory of Magnitude proposing shared parietal mechanisms for number, time, and space
description: ATOM (A Theory of Magnitude) proposes that numerical quantity, time, and space share common parietal processing mechanisms, with (intra)parietal cortices supporting an overarching concept of magnitude in a generalized manner. The review cites brain imaging studies showing overlapping neurofunctional circuits across magnitude dimensions, including an fMRI study finding responses that "substantially overlap across all three magnitude dimensions" in right-lateralized regions including the IPS and insula. The review uses ATOM to interpret DD adults' deficits in conceptual size, duration, and length processing as non-numerical magnitude deficits.
requirements: Requires the assumption of a generalized magnitude system spanning numerical and non-numerical dimensions
constraints: The review notes some studies challenge the common magnitude system account, citing independent adaptation mechanisms for numerosity and size
target_learning_goals: numerical magnitude processing
non-numerical magnitude processing (time, space, size)
examples: The review interprets DD adults' preserved length processing alongside deficient duration processing as compatible with a non-symbolic magnitude deficit including numerosity and duration but excluding length

article_title: Different leaders: Emergent organizational and intellectual leadership in children’s collaborative learning groups
citation: E. M. Mercier, S. E. Higgins, Laura da Costa. (2014). Different leaders: Emergent organizational and intellectual leadership in children's collaborative learning groups. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9201-z
title: Attend to how students engage in collaborative tasks so all students participate in both the intellectual and organizational demands
description: Because emergent leadership in collaborative groups is systematically distributed, with intellectual and organizational roles often taken by different students, the article argues that "attention should be paid to how students are engaging in collaborative learning tasks to ensure all students participate in the intellectual as well as organizational demands of the task." Teachers monitoring group work should look beyond whether the task is organized smoothly and check that students who organize are also engaging in the intellectual work, and vice versa.
requirements: Teachers or designers must be able to observe or capture students' interactions during collaborative tasks to notice which students are making intellectual versus organizational moves.
constraints: Findings come from year six pupils working on mystery framework tasks in history and mathematics in English primary schools; the article notes outcomes were similar across groups in study one so leadership-outcome relations were not explored there.
target_learners: primary school students working in small collaborative groups
target_learning_goals: equitable participation in collaborative learning
engagement in both idea development and group organization
examples: In study one, Amy in the opening vignette organized participation and turn-taking but did less of the intellectual work and appeared somewhat confused by the final solution.

article_title: Patterns of action transitions in online collaborative problem solving: A network analysis approach
citation: Shupin Li · Johanna Pöysä-Tarhonen · Päivi Häkkinen (2022). Patterns of action transitions in online collaborative problem solving: A network analysis approach. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2022) 17:191–223 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09369-7
title: ATC21S framework distinguishing social and cognitive CPS skills enacted in dyadic computer-based assessment
description: The study's organizing framework, from the Assessment and Teaching of 21st Century Skills project (Hesse et al., 2015), divides CPS into two intertwined skill dimensions. In this framework, "social skills refer to the 'collaborative' part of CPS that is often enacted through social interactions with the paired partner, including participation, perspective taking, and social regulation. Cognitive skills, on the other hand, refer to the 'problem-solving' part of CPS, such as task regulation and knowledge building." The study operationalizes these as log-file indicators scored via Rasch modeling with WLE scores across four CPS tasks. It differs from the PISA 2015 framework, which does not separate social from cognitive skills in CPS tasks.
requirements: Log-file action data from computer-based CPS tasks that can be coded into indicators matching the framework's subskills (participation, perspective taking, social regulation, task regulation, knowledge building) for automated Rasch-based scoring.
constraints: Unlike the PISA 2015 CPS framework, this framework separates social skills from cognitive skills in CPS tasks; the authors treat social and cognitive skills as inherently intertwined.
target_learners: school students assessed in pairs in computer-based environments (sixth graders in this study)
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem solving skills, both social and cognitive
examples: Skill levels 1-6 were identified through weighted likelihood estimate (WLE) scores from four game-like ATC21S tasks: Laughing Clown, Sunflower, Hot Chocolate, and Olive Oil.

article_title: Metacognitive scaffolding in an innovative learning arrangement
citation: Molenaar, I., van Boxtel, C. A. M., & Sleegers, P. J. C. (2010). Metacognitive scaffolding in an innovative learning arrangement. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9154-1
title: Atgentschool dynamic scaffolding system with three-dimensional virtual agent in the Ontdeknet e-learning environment
description: Atgentschool delivered metacognitive scaffolds through a three-dimensional virtual agent powered by Living Actor technology, embedded in the Ontdeknet e-learning environment where triads collaborated with an external expert on a country-study assignment. An attention management system with three levels (input, reasoning, intervention) monitored students' attention focus from keyboard strokes, mouse movements and event information to determine when to send which scaffold. For each sub-assignment, orientation, planning and monitoring scaffolds were implemented, with students receiving a minimum of 12 scaffolds shown in text balloons, spoken aloud, and accompanied by animations and emotions.
requirements: An attention management system to determine when to send which scaffold based on students' attention focus
User input via four icons (a help question mark and three emotional icons) as additional input
constraints: Scaffolds were delivered only during the first two lessons of the eight-lesson experiment
Control triads saw the same virtual agent without metacognitive support to prevent a Hawthorne effect
target_learners: elementary school students in Grades 4-6 working in heterogeneous triads
target_learning_goals: orientation, planning and monitoring of collaborative inquiry assignments
examples: Scaffolds were triggered at sub-assignment selection (orientation), just before execution (planning), and upon saving (monitoring)

article_title: Evaluating fluid and crystallized abilities in the performance of an educational process
citation: Angel Blanch. (2015). Evaluating fluid and crystallized abilities in the performance of an educational process. Springer Verlag. http://hdl.handle.net/10459.1/48328
title: Match instructional structure to learner ability: higher structured instruction benefits lower-ability students, low structured instruction benefits higher-ability students
description: Drawing on aptitude-treatment interaction (ATI) theory, the article recommends tailoring instructional structure to learner aptitude. As stated, "higher structured instruction is more beneficial for students with lower ability, while low structured instruction is more beneficial for students with higher ability." The article adds that more anxious individuals may attain optimum learning in highly structured interventions, and that novel or complex goals and inductive, unstructured organization impose higher requirements on Gf, whereas tasks requiring modification of known schemes, particularly in the language domain, impose higher requirements on Gc.
requirements: Evaluation of learners' broad cognitive abilities (Gf and Gc) to inform the choice of instructional structure
constraints: The article notes this interaction is further influenced by task and/or situational variables as suggested by ATI theory
target_learners: Students differing in cognitive aptitude, including individuals with specific learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: Optimizing achievement in instructional interventions matched to learner aptitude profiles
examples: The article suggests learning goals that are novel or complex, or instruction with a more inductive or unstructured organization, may impose higher requirements on Gf

article_title: How do you feel during English class? Emotions and metacognition in primary school children learning English as a second language
citation: Palladino, P., Trotta, E., Bonvino, A., Carlucci, L., & Cottini, M. (2025). How do you feel during English class? Emotions and metacognition in primary school children learning English as a second language. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09414-4
title: Attend to metacognitive and emotional variables from the earliest stages of L2 instruction
description: Because metacognitive monitoring and control and achievement emotions predict L2 vocabulary learning from the very beginning of instruction, teachers of early L2 learning should give these variables explicit attention. The authors argue that understanding "the interplay between metacognition and emotions in learning may lead to a better perspective on school L2 learning of significant variables", and that these variables "may deserve better attention from teachers since they substantially contribute to the SRL process". The principle applies from the first stages of L2 learning in primary school.
requirements: Teachers need ways to observe or assess children's confidence judgments, control of performance, and boredom during L2 lessons.
constraints: The supporting evidence is a short-term longitudinal correlational study; the authors note longer-term studies are needed to trace developmental changes in L2 learning.
target_learners: primary school children beginning second language learning
target_learning_goals: English vocabulary acquisition
self-regulated learning in L2
examples: The study assessed 305 Italian 2nd and 3rd graders twice within one school year, showing metacognition and boredom predicted vocabulary growth from the earliest stage.

article_title: Is the perceptual disfluency effect moderated by working memory capacity? Direct replication of Lehmann et al. (2016)
citation: Sophia C. Weissgerber, Denia Indah Permatasari Terhorst, Ralf Rummer. (2024). Is the perceptual disfluency effect moderated by working memory capacity? Direct replication of Lehmann et al. (2016). Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09366-7
title: ATI account: WMC as a boundary condition of the perceptual disfluency effect (Lehmann et al.'s deeper-processing hypothesis)
description: Lehmann et al.'s aptitude-treatment interaction hypothesis holds that disfluent texts impose extra extraneous cognitive load on working memory, so "Only learners with a high WMC might have enough capacity for the higher ECL caused by less legible texts and could engage in deeper processing". Learners with low WMC cannot handle the increased ECL, cannot allocate germane resources, and their situational-model construction is hindered; with fluent material, high- and low-WMC learners should show similar outcomes. The present replication tested this hypothesis directly and found its data "are not indicative of WMC as a boundary condition moderating the disfluency effect on learning".
requirements: The hypothesis presupposes that perceptual disfluency increases extraneous cognitive load that competes with germane resources, per Cognitive Load Theory (Sweller et al., 2011)
constraints: The replication data do not support the hypothesis; the article questions its robustness and generalizability beyond the primary study
target_learners: learners studying expository texts, characterized by working memory capacity
target_learning_goals: retention, comprehension, and transfer of expository text material (time and date differences on earth)
examples: Lehmann et al. (2016) operationalized disfluency as a grey-scaled Haettenschweiler 12 pt font versus black Arial 12 pt, measured WMC with the Numerical Updating Memory subtest (Oberauer et al., 2000), and tested retention, comprehension, and transfer

article_title: The Double-Edged Interactions of Prompts and Self-efficacy
citation: Nadja Gentner & Tina Seufert. (2020). The Double-Edged Interactions of Prompts and Self-efficacy. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09227-7
title: Aptitude-treatment interaction perspective: state-like self-efficacy during learning as a moderator of instructional support effectiveness
description: The article applies aptitude-treatment interaction (ATI) research to motivational aptitudes, proposing that "instructional features are most effective for learners with certain characteristics" and that, unlike static aptitudes such as prior knowledge, motivational variables like self-efficacy are state-like and change over the learning process. It therefore argues learner characteristics should be assessed during learning, since learners experiencing high self-efficacy while learning might profit from prompts, whereas those experiencing low self-efficacy might need more explicit instructions. This framework motivates the study's moderation hypotheses.
requirements: Assessment of the learner characteristic (self-efficacy) during the learning process rather than only before it
constraints: The article notes motivational or emotional aptitudes were largely neglected in prior ATI research, and that classic ATI aptitudes are assumed static over the whole learning process
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategy use and learning outcomes in hypermedia environments
examples: The study measured self-efficacy before, 20 minutes into, and directly after a 40-minute hypermedia learning session and tested moderation of prompt effects on outcomes and strategy use
key_sources: Nadja Gentner & Tina Seufert. (2020). The Double-Edged Interactions of Prompts and Self-efficacy. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09227-7

article_title: The Effects of Mobile-Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning: Meta-Analysis and Critical Synthesis
citation: Sung Yao-Ting, Yang Je-Ming, Lee Han-Yueh. (2017). The Effects of Mobile-Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning: Meta-Analysis and Critical Synthesis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317704307
title: AT-mCSCL framework: an activity-theory model of six elements for analyzing mobile-computer-supported collaborative learning
description: The AT-mCSCL framework is an activity-theory-based model, adapted from Engestrom (1987) and revised versions for mobile learning, that the authors propose "for further illustrating the mediating effects of some moderator variables between tools (i.e., the mobile devices) and the objective (i.e., the outcomes) of mCSCL research." It comprises six primary elements: tools/instruments, subjects, objectives, rules/control, context, and communication/interaction. The interactive connections among the elements form triangles (e.g., tools–rules/control–objectives) that the authors used to select moderator variables for the meta-analysis, such as subjects, rules/control, context, and communication/interaction.
requirements: Studies must be analyzable in terms of the six elements (tools/instruments, subjects, objectives, rules/control, context, communication/interaction) for the framework to structure coding of moderator variables.
constraints: The article presents the framework as a notional model for illustrating mediating effects, used to choose moderating variables, not as a tested causal model in itself.
target_learners: Students across learning stages from kindergarten to adults participating in mCSCL activities
target_learning_goals: Knowledge creation, problem solving, sharing/interaction, and learning motivation in collaborative settings
examples: The authors used the framework's triangles to organize the ten moderator variables coded in the meta-analysis, mapping each moderator to a tools–element–objectives triangle in Figure 2.

article_title: Stressors and Turning Points in High School and Dropout
citation: Dupéré, V., Leventhal, T., Dion, E., Crosnoe, R., Archambault, I., & Janosz, M. (2014). Stressors and Turning Points in High School and Dropout: A Stress Process, Life Course Framework. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Stressors+and+Turning+Points+in+High+School+and+Dropout
title: Support students during periods of heightened vulnerability triggered by proximal stressors, not only via early prevention
description: Because dropout can be precipitated by circumstances emerging late in schooling careers, the article argues that prevention should not rest solely on early intervention for long-term risk. Attention to "precipitating factors among students following a recognizable long-term problematic path could contribute to a better understanding of when (if ever) and under what circumstances high-risk students decide to stop attending school," helping pinpoint periods of increased vulnerability needing heightened attention. Non-typical dropouts who lack prior problem histories currently fly under the radar and receive limited support.
requirements: Capacity to detect students experiencing acute stressful circumstances during high school, including those without prior academic or behavioral problems
constraints: The article states precipitating events may matter more for the timing than the occurrence of dropout among students already on a problematic track
target_learners: high school students experiencing acute life stressors
target_learning_goals: school perseverance
timely identification of dropout risk
examples: The review cites early childhood education programs as relatively effective for high-risk youth while arguing this alone misses late-onset pathways

article_title: When personal becomes relational: A meta-analysis and narrative review on personality traits and children's affective relationships with adults
citation: Du, Q., Roorda, D. L., Koomen, H. M. Y., Jak, S., & Zee, M. (2025). When personal becomes relational: A meta-analysis and narrative review on personality traits and children's affective relationships with adults. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2025.100688
title: Attend to the personality traits of children and adults when seeking to understand children's affective relationships with adults
description: The article proposes that focusing on personality — of children, parents, and teachers, and of their similarity — is a useful lens for understanding the affective quality of adult–child relationships across contexts. It concludes that "focusing on personality may be a promising way to better understand children's affective relationships with adults in various contexts (e.g., family, school)." The recommendation rests on the meta-analytic and narrative findings that traits of both dyad members relate to relationship quality.
requirements: Practitioners or researchers need information on the personality traits of both the child and the adult in the dyad, since traits of both were associated with relationship quality.
constraints: The authors note the associations were "small to medium in magnitude", so personality is one factor among others rather than a decisive determinant.
target_learners: children in family and school contexts
target_learning_goals: understanding and supporting the affective quality of parent–child and teacher–child relationships
examples: The meta-analysis of k = 39 studies linked children's and parents' traits to parent–child relationship quality, and narrative reviews extended the pattern to teacher–child relationships and personality similarity.

article_title: How Learners Use Their Hands for Learning: an Eye-Tracking Study
citation: Babette Park · Andreas Korbach · Paul Ginns · Roland Brünken. (2023). How Learners Use Their Hands for Learning: an Eye-Tracking Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09833-2
title: Attention-directing explanation of the tracing effect (near-hand prioritization)
description: The article presents an explanation derived from basic cognitive science research on near-hand effects: hand position and activity fundamentally affect cognitive processes, so touch-based actions direct and focus visual attention on relevant material. The article states that "Near-hand position should evoke faster target detection and effective direction of attention, as well as potent shielding of attention from interferences." Under this view, learning benefits should specifically appear in recall-type performance such as remembering new terminologies or identifying recently learned contents, and not necessarily in comprehension. The present experiment was designed to test this explanation against the multimodal memory model via hypotheses H1a–H1c.
requirements: Learning material with separable text and illustration elements whose corresponding parts learners can point at or trace over with the index finger
constraints: Some studies on near-hand effects show the fragility of this effect (Andringa et al., 2018; Dosso & Kingstone, 2018), and reduced semantic processing of near-hand information has been reported (Davoli et al., 2010)
Yeo and Tzeng (2019) suggest tracing may only affect learning with highly visuospatial-based material
target_learners: School students learning from multimedia lessons
target_learning_goals: Retention and identification of newly learned terms from text-and-illustration lessons
examples: The present study operationalized this explanation as H1a–H1c, predicting higher performance, cognitive activity, and visual attention in both touch-based groups versus the no-touch group with no pointing–tracing difference

article_title: Toward Synergizing Educational Research and Movement Sciences: a Dialogue on Learning as Developing Perception for Action
citation: Dor Abrahamson · Franz Mechsner. (2022). Toward Synergizing Educational Research and Movement Sciences: a Dialogue on Learning as Developing Perception for Action. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09668-3
title: Attentional anchor: a strategically useful imaginary or real Gestalt that orients perception to facilitate goal movement
description: The attentional anchor is a hypothetical construct from enactivist theory denoting a strategically useful imaginary Gestalt, such as a diagonal line between the hands, that learners generate to solve motor-control problems. The article defines it as something that "orients, focalizes, and shapes perception toward an environment to facilitate the situated enactment of some goal movement form". It serves as the central ontological innovation linking Abrahamson's mathematics-education program with Mechsner's movement science, and the authors propose that any purposeful movement may be tacitly guided by such anchors.
requirements: A challenging movement task with feedback that makes perceptual solutions functionally necessary before formal instruction
constraints: The construct arose from controlled experimental conditions of the Mathematics Imagery Trainer; its generality to every learned movement is stated as a hypothesis, not an established finding
target_learners: elementary, secondary, and tertiary students learning mathematics concepts
target_learning_goals: grounding mathematical concepts such as proportionality, trigonometry, and parabolas in perceptuomotor coordination
examples: Lars's imaginary diagonal line guiding proportional bimanual coordination; imagined 12 o'clock and 9 o'clock marks guiding 90° phase-shifted circling; a parabola emerging as the anchor for moving in green along a screen

article_title: When Does Learning by Non-interactive Teaching Work? A Large-Scale Analysis of Learner Characteristics in a Classroom Setting
citation: Lachner, A., Russ, H., Hübner, N., Sibley, L., & Scheiter, K. (2025). When Does Learning by Non-interactive Teaching Work? A Large-Scale Analysis of Learner Characteristics in a Classroom Setting. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10060-0
title: Aptitude-treatment interaction framework applied to non-interactive teaching via a competence-oriented approach
description: The article organizes its moderation analysis around the aptitude-treatment interaction (ATI) paradigm, which "states that the effectiveness of an intervention can be conceptualized as a result of the complex interplay between the distinct features of the intervention and students' ability and willingness to utilize them". It extends this with a competence-oriented approach following Weinert, treating (meta-)cognitive and motivational dispositions as competence and demographic background and personality traits as precursors, testing nine learner characteristics simultaneously in a multilevel IPD framework.
requirements: Well-powered samples, since ATI effects are subtle and prior small-sample studies produced inconsistent findings
constraints: Prior ATI evidence in non-interactive teaching was inconsistent, with non-significant or even reversed findings across studies
target_learners: secondary physics students in grades 7 and 8
target_learning_goals: scientific understanding of optics (converging lens image formation)
metacognitive monitoring accuracy
examples: The study tested prior knowledge, academic self-concept, interest in physics, interest in technology, conscientiousness, gender, mother tongue, and socio-economic status simultaneously as moderators.

article_title: Short-Term Exposure to Nature and Benefits for Students’ Cognitive Performance: a Review
citation: Lucia Mason, Angelica Ronconi, Sara Scrimin, Francesca Pazzaglia. (2022). Short-Term Exposure to Nature and Benefits for Students' Cognitive Performance: a Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09631-8
title: Attention Restoration Theory: nature restores directed attention through soft fascination
description: Attention restoration theory (ART; Kaplan, 1995) explains the salutary effects of nature on cognitive functioning. It distinguishes involuntary attention, which is automatic and requires no mental resources, from voluntary or directed attention, which is effortful, goal-directed, and susceptible to fatigue. Restorative environments generate "soft fascination" as they gently attract involuntary attention without overwhelming the attentional system, allowing directed attention to rest and recover. The review uses ART as the main framework for interpreting cognitive benefits of green exposure.
requirements: Exposure to a natural environment rich in stimuli that softly capture involuntary attention, minimizing the need for voluntary attention
constraints: Urban environments have only poor restorative power because their bottom-up stimuli require directed attention to be overcome
target_learners: students at all educational levels, from elementary school to university
target_learning_goals: restoration of directed attention supporting executive functioning and self-regulation

article_title: What Are Teacher–Student Relationships in Adolescent Motivation Research? A Systematic Review of Conceptualizations, Measurement, and Analysis
citation: Emma C. Burns · Penny Van Bergen. (2025). What Are Teacher–Student Relationships in Adolescent Motivation Research? A Systematic Review of Conceptualizations, Measurement, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09998-y
title: Attachment theory conceptualizes teacher–student relationships as multidimensional bonds comprising closeness, conflict, and dependency
description: Attachment theory, one of three relational theories consistently employed in adolescent motivation research, argues that positive and secure emotional bonds are critical to adaptive functioning. Within it, "teacher–student relationships are multidimensional and can be considered via three dimensions: closeness, conflict, and dependency", with positive relationships high in closeness and low in conflict and dependency. More recent work attends to relationships outside a positive–negative binary, including complicated and reserved relationships.
requirements: Measurement should treat closeness and conflict as separate but co-occurring dimensions of the same relationship
constraints: The relevance of dependency in adolescence has been debated, with suggestions that teachers as a safe haven may not be developmentally appropriate
target_learning_goals: Academic motivation supported by positive teacher–student relationships
examples: The review notes adolescent motivation research often references attachment theory to support hypotheses but has not typically operationalized and integrated it with motivation theory

article_title: A latent profile analysis of math achievement, numerosity, and math anxiety in twins.
citation: Hart, Sara A.; Logan, Jessica A.R.; Thompson, Lee; Kovas, Yulia; McLoughlin, Gráinne; & Petrill, Stephen A. (2015). A latent profile analysis of math achievement, numerosity, and math anxiety in twins. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000045
title: Attentional control theory as an account of the math anxiety–achievement link
description: The article invokes attentional control theory (Eysenck & Calvo, 1992; Eysenck et al., 2007) to explain how math anxiety harms math performance: anxiety directs attention away from the goal toward threat-related stimuli, and 'These ruminations occupy the working memory system, and because math achievement is highly dependent on working memory, math achievement suffers.' The theory predicts anxiety should impair complex skills like math achievement but not basic skills like numerosity, which the LPA results were interpreted as supporting.

constraints: The article presents this as an interpretive account; the study design does not establish the causal mechanism
target_learners: school-age children and adolescents learning mathematics
target_learning_goals: math achievement
examples: Class 5 children had typical numerosity but low achievement with the highest math anxiety, which the authors read as consistent with the theory

article_title: Effects of discipline techniques on children's personality trait inferences.
citation: Rice, W. K., Jr. (1973). Effects of Discipline Techniques on Children's Personality-Trait Inferences. Ph.D. dissertation, The University of Oklahoma. University Microfilms No. 74-12,322. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Effects+of+Discipline+Techniques+on+Children%27s+Personality-Trait+Inferences
title: Kelley's attribution theory and its discounting principle as the explanatory framework for peer trait inferences from discipline episodes
description: The article adopts Kelley's informational-processing model of attribution theory, in which observers use the covariation principle with multiple observations and the discounting principle with a single observation: "The role of a given cause in producing a given effect is discounted if other Plausible causes are also present". Under minimal information, trait attribution is greatest when external causes are minimal, and negative information is weighted more heavily than positive. The study uses this framework to predict that approval-focused desists, whose negative content targets the child, yield more negative and more confident trait inferences.
requirements: Applies when the observer has only a single observation or minimal information about the behavior and its possible causes
constraints: When observers have information from multiple observations, the covariation principle applies and different results might be obtained
target_learning_goals: forming trait inferences about peers and teachers from observed social interactions
examples: The dissertation tested the framework's prediction with a tape-recording experiment in which observers heard either approval-focused or task-focused desists and rated the child and teacher on trait and confidence scales

article_title: The Devious Path of Slow Work.
citation: Bird, Grace E. (1921). The Devious Path of Slow Work. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ123456
title: Encourage learners to attain standard speed of motions as early as possible.
description: Bird, drawing on Gilbreth's motion study, argues that because "fast motions are different in character from slow motions," the learner "should be encouraged to attain standard speed of motions as early as possible." If motions cannot be made at standard speed by the beginner, rapidity should approach that of the expert, since habits initiated slowly may later cause retroactive inhibition when speed is sought.
requirements: Work should be provided in which the finest quality is not essential, so the beginner can approximate standard speed.
constraints: Undue haste can arouse anxiety, fear, or annoyance which interfere with rational processes; standard speed is not always high speed.
target_learning_goals: accurate and rapid execution of learned procedures
examples: Bird suggests that in arithmetic, approximations of the answer rather than exact results give the child opportunity to attain initial speed, paralleling the industrial beginner given work where fine quality is not essential.

article_title: Electrocortical correlates of attention differentiate individual capacity in associative learning
citation: Raynal, E., Schipper, K., Brandner, C., Ruggeri, P. & Barral, J. (2024). Electrocortical correlates of attention differentiate individual capacity in associative learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00236-8
title: Attentional-efficiency account of individual differences in associative learning
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that individual differences in associative learning arise from differences in how efficiently learners engage attentional processes. Across three EEG signatures, the authors report that "better learners engage attentional processes more eﬃciently than weaker learners, making more resources available", with increased functional activity in early attentional regions (precuneus, BA 7) and decision-making regions (frontal BA 11). The framework links P1, P3b and occipital GFP effects into a proposed sequence from early attentional processing through object recognition to frontal attentional control.
requirements: EEG recording during an associative learning task, analyzed with topographic (TANCOVA), Global Field Power, and sLORETA source-estimation methods
constraints: Whether individual differences reflect differences in the timing of the same processes or in the nature of the processes themselves remains unresolved
Overlapping GFP and TANCOVA results make it challenging to pinpoint the exact sequence of neural events
Findings are from young adults on a visual associative task; generalizability to other populations, learning types and modalities is untested
target_learning_goals: associative learning performance variability
examples: The authors propose the frontoparietal network's role in top-down regulation of attention could help better learners discriminate targets from lures in the task

article_title: Disentangling sensory precision and prior expectation of change in autism during tactile discrimination
citation: Sapey-Triomphe, L.-A., Sanchez, G., Hénaff, M.-A., Sonié, S., Schmitz, C., & Mattout, J. (2023). Disentangling sensory precision and prior expectation of change in autism during tactile discrimination. npj Science of Learning, 8:54. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00207-5
title: Refined predictive-coding account of ASD: atypical perceptual learning dynamics rather than a static prior/sensory imbalance
description: The article proposes that ASD is better characterized by the dynamic adjustment of precision weights to context than by a static imbalance between prior and sensory precision. It defines the sensory precision πu, the precision ratio r = πu/πx, and a response bias parameter b in a dynamic perceptual decision-making model, and argues that "these results point to atypical perceptual learning rather than altered perceptual inference per se". The account subsumes the observed no, normal, or slower adaptation depending on context.
requirements: Combining behavioral tasks sensitive to sensory precision and the precision ratio with computational modeling of trial-to-trial responses
constraints: Findings concern autistic adults without intellectual disability in low-level tactile frequency discrimination tasks; the authors call for further empirical and computational studies to refine predictive coding theories
target_learning_goals: implicit perceptual learning of stimulus statistics
adjustment of precision weights to context

article_title: Using virtual reality to study spatial mapping and threat learning
citation: Marino, C. E., Rjabtsenkov, P., Sharp, C., Ali, Z., Pineda, E., Bavdekar, S. Y., Garg, T., Jordan, K., Halvorsen, M., Aponte, C., Blue, J., Zhu, X. & Suarez-Jimenez, B. (2025). Using virtual reality to study spatial mapping and threat learning. npj Science of Learning 10:14. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00305-6
title: Attentional control theory account: state anxiety disrupts spatial mapping by diverting attention toward threat
description: The article uses attentional control theory as its explanatory framework for why some participants fail contextual threat learning. Under this account, "anxiety may impair performance via increased competition among attentional resources, thereby reducing attention to the ongoing task". Applied here, transient state anxiety in uncertain situations allocates attention toward threat detection and away from the environmental context — landmarks and location cues — needed to build a cognitive map, so non-learners lack an accurate mental representation of which zones predict shock. The authors also offer a competing explanation: anxiety-driven compensatory attention to potential threats may bias attention away from the actually predictive context.
requirements: The task must require attention to contextual and spatial cues (landmarks, zones) for successful discrimination, as the VR flower-picking paradigm does.
constraints: The authors state that deficits in discrimination learning in non-learners cannot be solely explained by heightened anxiety during the task; attention allocation was not assessed in this study, and the study did not assess trauma or other potential channels of learning.
target_learners: Healthy adult students navigating virtual environments
target_learning_goals: Learning to discriminate threat from safety based on contextual location cues
Forming accurate spatial/cognitive maps of an environment
examples: The VR conditioning task required participants to use local and distal landmarks to infer which half of the environment predicted shocks; non-learners failed this discrimination while showing higher state anxiety.

article_title: Insights from 200+ years of personalized learning
citation: David Dockterman. (2018). Insights from 200 + years of personalized learning. npj Science of Learning 3:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0033-x
title: Aptitude–Treatment Interaction (ATI) as a framework for matching instruction to learner variability
description: The article presents ATI, launched by Cronbach and Snow in the 1970s, as a research approach bringing rigor to studying the intersection of learner and instruction. It recognizes that learners differ cognitively, psychologically, and environmentally, so individuals respond differently to tasks and instruction forms, and "the same learner might respond to the same intervention differently under different environmental or psychological conditions." ATI laid foundations for computer-based adaptive learning by organizing efforts to match treatment to student need under optimal conditions.
requirements: Methodological techniques for determining the most effective match for each student, as ATI is said to have described
constraints: The article states the combinations of potential variables and treatments were, according to Cronbach and Snow, "virtually inexhaustible"
target_learners: all learners, across cognitive, psychological, and environmental difference dimensions
target_learning_goals: matching instructional methods to individual learner aptitudes and conditions
examples: The article credits ATI's expansive view of learner aptitudes with elevating psychological needs, such as social-emotional competencies, to central instructional considerations

article_title: Exams at classroom have bidirectional effects on the long-term memory of an unrelated graphical task
citation: P. Lopes da Cunha, D. Ramirez Butavand, L. B. Chisari, F. Ballarini and H. Viola (2018). Exams at classroom have bidirectional effects on the long-term memory of an unrelated graphical task. npj Science of Learning 3:19. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0036-7
title: Schedule exams attentively relative to other teaching, since exams modulate retention of temporally adjacent content
description: The authors recommend that educators consider when exams fall within the school day, because an exam can improve or impair retention of unrelated content learned up to about one hour before or after it. As they conclude, "educators should be attentive to their student's exams' schedule, as this will modulate the retention of the contents of previous or later teaching." The recommendation follows directly from the bidirectional timing effects observed.
requirements: Knowledge of when exams and other learning activities occur within the same school day
constraints: Effects were observed for exams occurring within about one hour before or after the unrelated learning; exams 4 h before or after showed no effect
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of curricular content learned in the classroom
examples: Students who took an exam 1 h after copying a figure showed improved 24-h retention if their retention was weak, and impaired retention if it was strong

article_title: “You did incredibly well!”: teachers’ inflated praise can make children from low-SES backgrounds seem less smart (but more hardworking)
citation: Schoneveld, E., & Brummelman, E. (2023). "You did incredibly well!": teachers' inflated praise can make children from low-SES backgrounds seem less smart (but more hardworking). npj Science of Learning, 8:31. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00183-w
title: Attribution-theory account of inflated praise as an inequality-reinforcing mechanism
description: The article builds on attribution theory, in which attributions reflect locus, stability, and controllability, and ability and effort are compensatory internal causes of success. It theorizes that teachers, influenced by negative stereotypes about low-SES children's abilities, attribute low-SES students' successes to "hard work" and thus give them more inflated praise, which children in turn interpret as a sign of low ability. The article identifies "effort attributions as a possible mechanism" linking teacher bias to inequality-reinforcing feedback.
requirements: Teachers must perceive a student's success as particularly praiseworthy due to presumed high effort for inflated praise to be dispensed
constraints: The mechanism was tested with hypothetical vignettes rather than real teacher-student interactions
Effects were probably larger than they would be in real life, per the authors
target_learning_goals: Academic ability perceptions and motivation in classroom feedback contexts
examples: Study 1 measured teachers' open-ended attributions of student success after vignettes; Study 2 measured children's smartness and effort inferences after praise vignettes
